title: Harvard Engineers Bacteria to Pull CO2 From Air Into Seawater 2.6 Times Faster
excerpt: A genetically modified marine bacterium accelerates rock weathering by stripping rust from mineral surfaces, offering a new biological pathway for industrial-scale carbon removal.
body:
• Harvard and Stanford researchers engineered a marine bacterium, Alteromonas macleodii, to speed up rock weathering by 2.6 times, boosting atmospheric CO2 removal into seawater.
  • The breakthrough, published in Nature Biotechnology, works by "de-rusting" mineral surfaces — the engineered bacteria produce siderophores continuously, unlike wild strains that stop once they have enough iron.
  • Pilot-scale bioreactors using olivine sand and Boston Harbor seawater captured 0.5 grams of atmospheric CO2 per day, providing proof that synthetic biology can accelerate a geological process.
  • Researchers envision scaling the technology in large basins similar to sewage treatment plants, pumping seawater through engineered bacterial cultures to sequester carbon at industrial scale.

Speeding Up a Geological Thermostat

Rock weathering — the slow dissolution of minerals by water, air, and biological activity — is one of Earth's fundamental carbon regulators. Over hundreds of thousands of years, dissolved silicate minerals wash into the ocean, trapping atmospheric CO2 as bicarbonate and gradually cooling the planet. Scientists have long asked whether this natural thermostat could be accelerated to fight climate change.

A team at Harvard's Wyss Institute, Harvard Medical School, and the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability has now demonstrated one approach: genetically engineered bacteria that speed up the process by 2.6 times. Their findings, published in Nature Biotechnology, represent the first proof that synthetic biology can meaningfully accelerate enhanced rock weathering for carbon removal.

The Rust Problem

When silicate minerals like olivine dissolve in water, they release magnesium, iron, and silicate, converting atmospheric CO2 into bicarbonate. But there is a catch. The released iron oxidizes when exposed to air, forming rust that coats the mineral surface and slows further dissolution — a bottleneck that has limited the viability of enhanced rock weathering at industrial scale.

Some marine bacteria naturally produce molecules called siderophores that strip this rust, solubilizing the iron for their own growth. But the researchers, led by first author Neil Dalvie and faculty members Pamela Silver and Michael Springer, discovered a critical limitation: wild bacteria stop producing siderophores the moment they have enough iron.

"Once wild bacteria have enough iron to grow, they stop making siderophores completely. To enable enhanced weathering at scale, we engineered A. macleodii to always produce siderophores. We essentially decoupled siderophore production from environmental iron levels."

— Neil Dalvie, First Author, Wyss Institute at Harvard University

From Lab Bench to Pilot Scale

The team genetically modified Alteromonas macleodii, a widespread marine bacterium, to continuously produce siderophores regardless of iron availability. Engineering the microbes took roughly a month. Proving they worked took considerably longer.

Initial experiments used eVOLVER bioreactors — small-scale devices designed by Wyss Institute faculty member Ahmad Khalil — with seawater continuously flowing over minerals. When results looked promising, the team scaled up to pilot-size bioreactors loaded with several kilograms of green olivine sand submerged in raw seawater collected from Boston Harbor.

The pilot system captured 0.5 grams of atmospheric CO2 per day — a modest number in absolute terms, but a compelling validation that the biological intervention works at a measurable scale. The team also conducted a life-cycle analysis with Stanford collaborators to calculate the net carbon balance of the entire system, identifying which operating parameters would matter most at industrial scale.

The Path to Industrial Deployment

Scaling from pilot bioreactors to climate-relevant impact is the next challenge. The researchers envision growing engineered bacteria in large basins resembling sewage treatment facilities, with unprocessed seawater pumped continuously through the system. The alkaline, carbon-rich water would be released back into the ocean, where the sequestered carbon would remain stable as dissolved bicarbonate.

"We believe this easily applicable, risk-free environmental engineering strategy could be implemented at many places with real-world decarbonization outcomes," said Silver, who is the Elliot T. and Onie H. Adams Professor of Biochemistry and System Biology at Harvard Medical School.

Several hurdles remain. The team needs to identify economically viable sources of silicate minerals and feedstocks for the bacteria. They are also exploring whether valuable metals could be extracted from the minerals as a co-product alongside carbon sequestration — a potential revenue stream that could improve the economics of deployment.

Why It Matters

Enhanced rock weathering has attracted significant commercial interest, with multiple startups already scattering crushed silicate rocks on agricultural surfaces. But the process has been too slow for meaningful climate impact. By using synthetic biology to remove the iron-passivation bottleneck, the Harvard-Stanford team has opened a biological pathway to acceleration that does not rely on higher temperatures or more energy-intensive grinding.

Dalvie recently received a Burroughs Wellcome Career Award to continue work on microbial siderophore production and mineral processing, signaling ongoing momentum behind the approach.
image_caption: Engineered bacteria designed for carbon capture. Harvard researchers modified E. coli bacteria to pull carbon dioxide from air into seawater at 2.6 times the natural rate.
nri_angle: The research involves Indian-origin scientist Amogh Jalihal as co-author, and the carbon removal technology has implications for India's climate commitments and coastal infrastructure.
